Configurable System: Digital-twin enabled system (DTES) for personalized wearable medical devices; demonstrated with a triaxial vibration collection bracelet prototype[1]
Domain Context: Healthcare (personalized healthcare; long-term care for elderly/disabled populations)[1]
Study Type: Design research with applied case study (three scenarios) combining DT services and wearable medical devices[1]
Conceptual Framework: Digital Twin–based personalization across the product cycle, connecting participants via cloud services and leveraging IoT/big data/AI for personalization[1]
Findings Implications: Bracelet demonstrated feasibility for end-to-end design/remote connection[1] and identified user motion parameters/patterns[1]; DTES showed high correlation in rehabilitation training (ρ=0.991) but lower in wheelchair experiment (ρ=0.749), indicating challenges in complex motion scenarios[1]; argues DT can enable personalized medicine[1]
User Population: Patients with chronic diseases and elderly; also targets elderly/disabled in long-term care contexts[1]
Personalization Method: User inputs parameter data; data extracted from cloud to generate CAD files as inputs for personalized manufacturing; prototype produced via 3D printing and assembly[1]
Citation: Zhengxu Zhu, Ray Y. Zhong. A digital twin enabled wearable device for customized healthcare. 2022.[1]

Configurable System: Modular healthcare services approach: service modules combined to create individualized patient pathways based on needs/preferences (demonstrated with use case + personas in colorectal cancer care)[2]
Domain Context: Healthcare services—oncology pathways (comprehensive cancer care network; colorectal cancer)[2]
Study Type: Design science research: iterative build and evaluation of healthcare-specific modularization parameters[2]
Conceptual Framework: Service modularization (decomposing services/processes into decoupled service modules with interfaces) and modularization parameters as assessment criteria[2]
Findings Implications: Argues modularization enables efficient individualized healthcare services[2]; provides a theoretical contribution (set of modularization parameters)[2] and calls for tools integrating these parameters to support modularization in practice[2]
User Population: Personas of colorectal cancer patients; involvement of oncology pathway domain experts[2]
Personalization Method: Modular component selection: modules selected for a persona ultimately form the pathway; reuse of modules across pathways is an intended effect[2]
Citation: Christoph Peters; Peggy Richter. Individualizing Patient Pathways through Modularization: Design and Evaluation of Healthcare-Specific Modularization Parameters.[2]

Configurable System: Method for defining product concepts with standardized, variant, and personalized characteristics for components; applied to a medical-device product family (flow diverter)[3]
Domain Context: Healthcare / medical devices (method focuses on medical devices)[3]
Study Type: Methodological design research: method for defining appropriate variety level for a product family, applied to a flow diverter example[3]
Conceptual Framework: Design for Variety approach with Tree of External Variety (TEV) and Variety Allocation Model (VAM) to assess differentiating properties, customer value, and complexity/personalization workload[3]
Findings Implications: Approach for determining customer value vs variety-induced complexity/personalization workload was shown suitable[3]; flow-diverter family could be structured into aneurysm/distal/proximal segments[3] and was applied successfully to the example product[3]
User Population: Physician and patient are collectively treated as the customer[3]
Personalization Method: Virtual segmentation[3] with individualized attributes such as proximal braid angle at positions[3] and proximal segment length defined per customer[3]
Citation: Design of Personalized Devices—The Tradeoff between Individual Value and Personalization Workload (Applied Sciences).[3]

Configurable System: DiaFit: interactive physical modular toolkit for assembling customizable Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) monitoring wearables from modular accessories/modules[4]
Domain Context: Healthcare—wearable devices for Type 1 Diabetes monitoring in everyday life contexts[4]
Study Type: Co-design/design research with prototype evaluation (evaluated with five participants)[4]
Conceptual Framework: Co-design approach[4] combined with modular design/modularity principles as a key practice[4]
Findings Implications: Identifies need for flexible/optional device use across contexts and highlights customization/DIY implications for wearable medical device design/evaluation[4]; participants were highly interested in customizing accessories/modules and creating combinations[4]
User Population: People with Type 1 Diabetes (adult participants)[4]
Personalization Method: Users assemble modular accessories and feedback modules to create different wearable forms (wrist/finger/ear/neck) with visual/audio/haptic feedback; modules can be modified/replaced/exchanged[4]
Citation: DiaFit: Designing Customizable Wearables for Type 1 Diabetes Monitoring.[4]

Configurable System: Modularized solid oral dosage-form product platform enabling reconfigurable assembly of module variants into individualized dosage forms[5]
Domain Context: Healthcare / pharmaceuticals—individualized pharmaceutical therapy via solid oral dosage forms[5]
Study Type: Experimental concept demonstration of modular dosage forms for multifunctional individualization[5]
Conceptual Framework: Product modularity[5], reconfigurable assembly of modules into products[5], positioned within mass customization/mass personalization framing[5]
Findings Implications: Three module variants produced three unique release profiles[5]; reconfiguration enabled six release-profile variants from only three module variants[5]; dose and release kinetics were a predictable net effect of constituent modules[5]
User Population: Patients (context is individualized pharmaceutical therapy; specific population not detailed)[5]
Personalization Method: Reconfigurable modular assembly (combining identical/dissimilar module variants) to increase variety[5]; uses spatial separation of dose- and release-controlling functions across module variants[5]
Citation: Rydvikha Govender, S. Abrahmsén-Alami, A. Larsson, Anders Borde, Alexander Liljeblad, S. Folestad. Independent Tailoring of Dose and Drug Release via a Modularized Product Design Concept for Mass Customization. Pharmaceutics, 2020.[5]

Configurable System: Open-design implementation and online collaborative design workflow to co-design a medication dispenser with a geographically dispersed community of people with cystic fibrosis (virtual meetings/workshops + prototype)[6]
Domain Context: Healthcare—medication management / product design for people with cystic fibrosis[6]
Study Type: Action research–oriented open-design case study (community development supported through tools and online workshops with a designer)[6]
Conceptual Framework: Open design approach; leverages knowledge/action of lead users for early-stage concept generation and continual evaluation[6]
Findings Implications: Open design can support early concept generation, continual evaluation, and innovation via lead-user knowledge/action[6]; paper also analyzes regulatory/implementation/economic challenges that pose barriers[6]
User Population: People with cystic fibrosis participating in online collaborative design[6]
Personalization Method: Participatory open-design co-creation through wholly virtual meetings/workshops empowering participants to conceive/develop products from lived experience[6]
Citation: Online open-design project to collaboratively design a medication dispenser for cystic fibrosis (full bibliographic details not included in provided excerpts).[6]

Configurable System: 3D-printed upper-limb/hand exoskeleton personalization pipeline combining vision-based and AI-based control across stages[7]
Domain Context: Healthcare; rehabilitation/assistive technology—upper limb exoskeletons for neuromotor rehabilitation[7]
Study Type: Experience-based applied review presenting possibilities/limitations and real-life examples/case studies of personalized 3D-printed exoskeletons[7]
Conceptual Framework: Standards/guidelines framing including AGREE II for guideline appraisal[7] and considerations linked to Industry 4.0/5.0 and ISO 27001 (and other standards noted)[7]
Findings Implications: States personalization improves usability/comfort of medical devices[7] and discusses possibilities/limitations of personalization for upper-limb exoskeletons[7]
User Population: Users include people with congenital defects, hand injuries, or post-stroke impairments; exoskeletons aim to restore upper-limb function and quality of life[7]
Personalization Method: Combined 3D scanning + 3D printing + reverse engineering + AI[7]; individualized functional assessment with AI-based selection of model/settings for each patient[7]; patient-tailored template-based exoskeleton design[7]
Citation: D. Mikołajewski, Izabela Rojek, P. Kotlarz, J. Dorożyński, J. Kopowski. Personalization of the 3D-Printed Upper Limb Exoskeleton Design—Mechanical and IT Aspects. Applied Sciences (Appl. Sci.), 2023.[7]

Configurable System: Participatory design of pediatric upper-limb prostheses producing modular prototypes (including adjustable wrist unit designed to work within a modular system)[8]
Domain Context: Assistive technology / healthcare—children and adolescents with upper-limb difference[8]
Study Type: Qualitative participatory design with multi-stage focus groups and semi-structured interviews plus iterative prototyping using 3D printing[8]
Conceptual Framework: BRIDGE methodology for involving children as equal stakeholders in design (HCI child-centered participatory design methodology)[8]
Findings Implications: Study identified improvement areas from children/adolescents’ perspectives and iterated prototypes with feedback[8]; future development should focus on ease of use, versatility, appearance, and safety[8]
User Population: 34 participants: children aged 8–15 with upper-limb difference plus parents, prosthetists, and occupational therapists[8]
Personalization Method: Iterative rapid prototyping (3D printing) within BRIDGE to develop modular, task-specific devices that provide user choice and support customisable solutions[8]
Citation: T. Sims, A. Cranny, C. Metcalf, P. Chappell, M. Donovan-Hall. PARTICIPATORY DESIGN OF PEDIATRIC UPPER LIMB PROSTHESES: QUALITATIVE METHODS AND PROTOTYPING. 2017.[8]

Configurable System: Fit for Purpose (F4P) modular 3D-printed terminal-device prosthesis prototypes (passive hand + functional prehensor), developed from shared CAD files (Fusion 360) and fabricated via 3D printing[9]
Domain Context: Assistive technology—upper-limb prosthetics for LMIC contexts (Uganda)[9]
Study Type: Applied co-design case study: co-design activities in Uganda driving two prototypes; includes prototyping/printing evaluations[9]
Conceptual Framework: Patient and Public Involvement and Engagement (PPIE) and codesign for LMIC prosthesis design; discrete choice approach used in co-design activity[9]
Findings Implications: Local participation provides rich feedback on what’s integral for acceptable prosthetic solutions in Uganda[9]; co-design workshops enabled users to input as designs evolved[9]; 3D printing has potential in LMICs but is not sufficient alone to benefit users (needs broader infrastructure/process support)[9]
User Population: Participants (n=17) involved in co-design; target includes unilateral adult transradial users[9]
Personalization Method: Modularity enabled via standard socket thread (1/2-20) allowing use across levels of upper-limb loss[9]; iterative co-design to refine aesthetics/acceptability[9]; distributed fabrication supported by sharing print settings/model files[9]
Citation: A. Hussaini, P. Kyberd, B. Mulindwa, R. Ssekitoleko, W. Keeble, L. Kenney, David Howard. 3D Printing in LMICs: Functional Design for Upper Limb Prosthetics in Uganda. 2023.[9]

Configurable System: Bespoke assistive-technology co-design service producing reconfigurable CAD + additive-manufactured devices with dimensions that can be changed/reconfigured for different users[10]
Domain Context: Assistive technology in healthcare/rehabilitation services (Swansea Rehabilitation Engineering Unit, UK NHS)[10]
Study Type: Service evaluation reporting three case studies of co-design for customized assistive devices within a healthcare rehabilitation engineering department[10]
Conceptual Framework: Co-design/participatory design methodology involving end users through iterative collaboration; user feedback drives subsequent iterations[10]
Findings Implications: Participants were satisfied with devices and the service[10]; bespoke devices helped overcome challenges and provided broader physical/mental wellbeing benefits[10]; participants valued involvement and saw their feedback ensure customization to needs[10]
User Population: Adults (18+) living with long-term chronic health conditions (three participants)[10]
Personalization Method: Design requirements and ideas generated via sketches/low-fidelity prototypes[10]; functional prototypes created using CAD and additive manufacturing[10] and posted to participants for real-world trial/iteration[10]
Citation: Assessing the use of co-design to produce bespoke assistive technology solutions within a current healthcare service: a service evaluation.[10]

Configurable System: Remote co-creation workflow for co-manufacturing a custom spoon handle with people with disabilities (digital manufacturing centered around videoconferencing from design to final 3D printing)[11]
Domain Context: Assistive technology / rehabilitation—co-creating assistive devices with rehabilitation professionals[11]
Study Type: Workflow description and feasibility-oriented case study showcasing co-manufacturing with two participants with cerebral palsy[11]
Conceptual Framework: Not mentioned in source.
Findings Implications: Involving people with disabilities in co-creation opens opportunities for healthcare providers and should be explored further using the described methodology[11]; may yield therapeutic benefits and needs actions for clinical viability[11]; standard questionnaires can measure effectiveness/satisfaction and guide design efforts[11]
User Population: Two people with cerebral palsy[11]
Personalization Method: Customization via videoconferenced co-design/co-manufacturing and 3D printing to produce a custom spoon handle[11]
Citation: From patient to maker - a workflow including people with cerebral palsy in co-creating assistive devices using 3D printing technologies.[11]

Configurable System: Technology Enriched Rehabilitation Gym (TERG): an eight-week technology-based rehabilitation programme delivered through commercial + prototype tech, serving as a participatory co-creation environment for rehabilitation technology[12]
Domain Context: Healthcare rehabilitation—stroke survivors with mobility/communication/cognitive disabilities[12]
Study Type: Participatory model description with two illustrative case studies showing devices benefitting from participatory co-creation approach[12]
Conceptual Framework: Double Diamond design process used in the design process[12] and MRC framework for design of complex medical interventions/devices used in a case study[12]
Findings Implications: Co-creation model produced five new technologies[12], accessibility modifications to existing technology (e.g., hand grips; rehab game structure)[12], and co-created protocols informed by feasibility/impact data[12]; feasibility of approach reported[12]
User Population: Participants living with stroke-related disabilities (mobility, communication, cognition)[12]
Personalization Method: Goal setting interview and baseline measures used to design an intensive personalized programme[12]; purposively selected focus groups (n=5–8) provide focused feedback on devices[12]; collaborative design led to mobile app + hardware system emphasizing social involvement and accessible peer support[12]
Citation: JMIR Preprints entry (DOI: https://doi.org/10.2196/preprints.57227); title and full bibliographic details not included in provided excerpts.[12]

Configurable System: vCare ICT platform: virtual coaching (VC) platform encapsulating coaching services to support personalized rehabilitation, evaluated through incremental phases (Tech Labs, Living Labs, Pilot Tests)[13]
Domain Context: Healthcare rehabilitation—tailored for stroke and Parkinson’s disease patients (and potentially cardiovascular patients)[13]
Study Type: Participatory/user-centered design experience report presenting methodology and preliminary user-feedback results for an ICT system evaluation[13]
Conceptual Framework: User-centered strategy with end-user involvement essential for co-design and evaluation; iterative feedback integrated throughout development[13]
Findings Implications: Positive user experience reported (UEQ median score > 1 across domains)[13] and high usability for overall system (82.28 ± 15.12)[13]; participatory activities intended to ensure final release matches user expectations[13]
User Population: 30 patients (14 post-stroke; 16 Parkinson’s), 13 healthy elderly, and 6 health professionals enrolled[13]
Personalization Method: Personalized rehabilitation treatments configured according to clinical status and clinician indications, using motor/cognitive serious games in VR[13]; activities organized into game packages with specific rehabilitation objectives and predefined game sets per aim[13]
Citation: Virtual Coaching for Rehabilitation: The Participatory Design Experience of the vCare Project.[13]

Configurable System: Victoria Hand Project (VHP): clinician-supported software workflow integrating 3D CAD for socket creation, plus modular prosthetic component system customized by selecting among many component options[14]
Domain Context: Assistive technology—upper-limb prosthetic provision (low-cost prosthetic applications)[14]
Study Type: Experiential case report describing VHP’s implementation, benefits, and challenges[14]
Conceptual Framework: Distributed partnership/service-delivery model: partners receive equipment, training, and ongoing support to provide prosthetic arms in their own clinics (local, sustainable care model)[14]
Findings Implications: Explores affordability/customization benefits and implementation challenges (quality control; learning curve for digital 3D workflows)[14]; partner feedback can trigger design changes that are built/tested centrally and pushed as updated digital files to partners via software[14]
User Population: People with upper-limb amputations receiving prostheses[14]; clinicians/prosthetists trained in rapid prototyping (50+ clinicians; 11 partnerships)[14]
Personalization Method: Modular selection of components (terminal devices, wrists, sockets, harness components)[14]; clinician-guided socket creation from 3D scans imported into VHP software[14]
Citation: Orthotics Journal. 2023; Volume 6, Issue 2, No. 9. (Article on Victoria Hand Project and impact of 3D printing.)[14]

Configurable System: Patient-centered design (PCD) implemented via computer-based cognitive prosthetics (CBCP) and a telerehabilitation delivery system combining software + videoconferencing for home treatment[15]
Domain Context: Healthcare rehabilitation—personalization of rehabilitation software for cognitive disabilities (traumatic brain injury case studies)[15]
Study Type: Design research describing PCD methodology and applied case studies in TBI rehabilitation[15]
Conceptual Framework: PCD integrates user-centered design (UCD) and participatory design (PD); involves clinicians, individuals with cognitive disabilities, and software designers as actors[15]
Findings Implications: UI is the principal design issue[15]; small UI changes can determine whether a system is usable[15]; users (including those with profound cognitive disabilities) can guide UI design for efficient interfaces[15]; PCD can promote clinical gains[15]
User Population: Individuals with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and cognitive disabilities; clinicians and software designers participate in PCD[15]
Personalization Method: PD approach enabling users to shape interface details[15]; strategy includes stripping down functionality to what’s needed for a given therapy session[15]; observational analysis identifies failures and yields personalized requirements for features/UI[15]
Citation: Patient-Centered Design: Interface Personalization for Individuals with Brain Injury (2011).[15]

Configurable System: COMPA (browser-extension support for AAC in remote meetings) and Speech Macros (purpose-driven shortcuts that generate sentences from brief input), developed and evaluated through multi-phase co-design and empirical studies[16]
Domain Context: Assistive technology—Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) support in remote meetings and conversations; includes motion-based expressive robotic objects as design material for AAC agency support[16]
Study Type: Design research dissertation combining empirical studies and participatory co-design (e.g., 12 adult AAC user study for LLM suggestions; multi-phase co-design workshops)[16]
Conceptual Framework: Agency in AAC design framework; defines conversational agency (technical vs colloquial) and investigates factors/measurement of agency in AAC[16]
Findings Implications: AAC users’ participation affected by conversational constraints and partner behavior (e.g., more frequent participation when directly addressed)[16]; participants were excited about AI-generated suggestions but stated requirements for usability[16]; COMPA features “leveled the playing field” by leveraging opportunities identified through the agency framework[16]
User Population: Expert augmented communicators (including people with cerebral palsy) and their close conversation partners (4 ACs + partners recruited), plus 12 adult AAC users for Speech Macros study[16]
Personalization Method: Users requested suggestions match personal style and be customizable/editable/removable[16]; Speech Macros use LLM prompting with examples/descriptions[16] and can incorporate user background/preferences (topics, partner-specific context)[16]
Citation: Stephanie Valencia. Agency in Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC). 2024.[16]

Configurable System: Inclusive participatory open-design assistive-device co-design approach using DIY as prototyping/communication/personal manufacturing process[17]
Domain Context: Community-based rehabilitation and assistive technology contexts[17]
Study Type: Design research describing an inclusive participatory design approach for open-design assistive devices[17]
Conceptual Framework: Co-construction theories[17] and flow experience framing[17]; DIY used as prototyping language and personal manufacturing process[17]
Findings Implications: Active engagement enables disabled people and carers to become conscious actors in maintaining well-being[17]; co-creation is used iteratively to steer the patient toward flow experiences[17]
User Population: Disabled users/patients and their dynamic environment[17]; caregivers, patients, and occupational therapists[17]
Personalization Method: DIY physical prototyping/personal manufacturing and iterative co-creation techniques grounded in co-construction to support user-driven customization[17]
Citation: Lieven De Couvreur, J. Detand, R. Goossens. The role of flow experience in codesigning open-design assistive devices. 2011.[17]

Configurable System: Practice-based co-construction of assistive artifacts through spontaneous collaboration and “design hacking” that blends design time and use time[18]
Domain Context: Community-based rehabilitation contexts[18]
Study Type: Practice-based case study[18]
Conceptual Framework: Evolutionary systematic worldview drawing on self-organization/adaptivity[18], plus concepts of stigmergic prototyping[18] and Maxwell’s Demon as a conceptual device[18]
Findings Implications: Emphasizes spontaneous local collaboration producing self-made assistive artifacts[18]; design hacking blurs design/use time[18] enabling co-evolution toward fit solutions[18]
User Population: Occupational therapists, professional non-designers, caregivers, and disabled people[18]
Personalization Method: Co-construction via stigmergic prototyping (including emotional seeding) and design hacking to support ongoing adaptation and customization in use contexts[18]
Citation: Lieven De Couvreur, J. Detand, W. Dejonghe, R. Goossens. Expect the unexpected: the co-construction of assistive artifacts. 2012.[18]

Configurable System: Meta-design framework for end-user development (EUD) illustrated via systems such as MAPS (caregiver-modifiable prompting environment) and TagTrainer (therapist-created rehabilitation exercises via Exercise Creator)[19]
Domain Context: Assistive technology/healthcare (cognitive disabilities as “universe of one”; rehabilitation clinics) plus other EUD domains (e-government)[19]
Study Type: Literature review and synthesis of meta-design as a framework for EUD, reviewing prior work and examples[19]
Conceptual Framework: Meta-design as a framework empowering stakeholders in continuous development of socio-technical systems[19]; includes methodologies/models such as Software Shaping Workshops (SSW)[19] and ICE2 model[19]
Findings Implications: Meta-design provides enabling conditions to put owners of problems in charge via technical/social conditions for broad participation[19]; identifies participation overload as a serious issue[19] and notes need to improve methods such as rich seeds/reuse/redesign/remixing to cope[19]
User Population: Caregivers[19], therapists[19], and additional stakeholder groups (e.g., civil servants in e-government EUD)[19]
Personalization Method: Toolkit/editor-based personalization: caregivers edit/store/reuse multimedia prompting scripts via an editor[19]; therapists create/modify exercises with TagTrainer Exercise Creator[19]; EUD via fill-in forms + wizard patterns in another example[19]
Citation: G. Fischer, D. Fogli, A. Piccinno. Revisiting and Broadening the Meta-Design Framework for End-User Development. 2017.[19]

Configurable System: Meta-design framework: creating socio-technical conditions so end users become co-designers of digital artifacts at use time; uses SER process model for evolving systems[20]
Domain Context: Foundational HCI/socio-technical systems theory; includes example scenario of smart home empowerment[20]
Study Type: Seminal conceptual framework paper defining meta-design objectives/techniques/processes for owners of problems to act as designers[20]
Conceptual Framework: Meta-design definition (owners of problems as designers)[20] and SER (Seeding, Evolutionary Growth, Reseeding) process model for evolving underdesigned “seeds” over time[20]
Findings Implications: Meta-design may augment participatory design by involving users at both design and use time to support EUD[20]; warns about tension between standardization and improvisation[20]
User Population: End users as “users-as-designers” who can engage in continuous development of systems they use[21, 20]
Personalization Method: EUD methods enable creation/extension/adaptation of artifacts[20]; users can customize over time (evolutionary growth)[20], often via graphical interfaces such as trigger-action rules[21]
Citation: G. Fischer, Elisa Giaccardi, Yunwen Ye, Alistair G. Sutcliffe, Nikolay Mehandjiev. Meta-design. 2004.[20]

Configurable System: Software Shaping Workshop (SSW): virtual workshop environments with familiar tools; provides each end-user community an “application workshop” for daily work[22]
Domain Context: Foundational meta-design/EUD methodology applied across domains (including medicine)[22]
Study Type: Conceptual framework paper describing a meta-design approach to bridge co-evolution and stakeholder communication gaps[22]
Conceptual Framework: Meta-design paradigm (owners of problems as designers)[22] combined with SER process model (seed creation, evolutionary growth, reseeding)[22] and an Interaction & Co-Evolution model[22]
Findings Implications: Approach aims to bridge communication gaps among stakeholders and transfer responsibility for system design/evolution to domain experts[22]; describes co-evolution via generation/request/exchange activities across SSW lifecycle[22]
User Population: End users as owners of problems[22], alongside software engineers and HCI experts[22]
Personalization Method: Application workshops customized to end users’ culture/background/skills and can be tailored by users via creating new artifacts[22]; users employ their own languages/notations in workshops[22]
Citation: M. Costabile, D. Fogli, R. Lanzilotti, A. Marcante, P. Mussio, L. P. Provenza, Antonio Piccinno. Meta-design to Face Co-evolution and Communication Gaps Between Users and Designers. 2007.[22]

Configurable System: Toolkits for user innovation: coordinated, “user-friendly” design toolsets enabling users to develop new product innovations for themselves (more capable than typical product configurators)[23]
Domain Context: Foundational innovation/production theory applicable to products/services where heterogeneous demand makes custom solutions valuable[23]
Study Type: Conceptual/theoretical paper explaining why/how toolkits for user innovation work[23]
Conceptual Framework: Task partitioning via toolkits: transfer need-related development tasks from manufacturers to users and equip users with tools; grounded in “information stickiness” concept[23]
Findings Implications: Assigning need-related tasks to users and solution-related tasks to manufacturers can compress time/cost and better integrate learning-by-doing[23]; toolkits can create competitive advantage for first movers[23]
User Population: Toolkit users can iteratively design/simulate/prototype and evaluate in their use environment[23]; example toolkit users include electrical engineers designing electronic systems with custom ICs[23]
Personalization Method: Users customize using module libraries within toolkits[23] and iteratively create/test/improve designs within customary language/representations[23]
Citation: von Hippel, E., & Katz, R. Shifting Innovation to Users via Toolkits. Management Science, 2002 (48(7)).[23]

Configurable System: Innovation toolkits in a real-world case: user modifications to open-source Apache security software; argues for toolkits to support user-designed customization[24]
Domain Context: Foundational toolkit evidence base (software domain; demonstrates heterogeneous needs and customization benefits)[24]
Study Type: Empirical study / case analysis of Apache security software users’ heterogeneous needs and modification behavior[24]
Conceptual Framework: Toolkits for user innovation as a hypothesized mechanism to increase satisfaction under heterogeneous needs conditions[24]
Findings Implications: Finds high heterogeneity of need and dissatisfaction with standard security functionality[24]; users who create their own modifications are significantly more satisfied[24]; hypothesizes toolkits enabling easier customization will increase satisfaction[24]
User Population: Apache users[24]
Personalization Method: User-driven customization through open-source software modification; proposes toolkits to make customization easier[24]
Citation: N. Franke, E. Hippel. Satisfying Heterogeneous User Needs via Innovation Toolkits: The Case of Apache Security Software. 2002.[24]

Configurable System: Online product configurators used in mass customization as co-creation tools; focuses on customer experience and reasons configurators fail in sales conversion[25]
Domain Context: Consumer products / mass customization market context[25]
Study Type: Empirical study investigating customer experience throughout the co-creation process[25]
Conceptual Framework: Customer co-creation experience framework identifying six factors influencing configurator experience (price, design freedom, information quality, product visualization, trust, individual differences)[25]
Findings Implications: Notes startup challenges (20% failure rate within 15 months)[25]; suggests balancing customization and simplicity improves satisfaction/engagement[25]; advanced visualization and a personal approach improve interaction with configurators[25]
User Population: Customers/consumers engaged in co-creation via configurators[25]
Personalization Method: Toolkits/configurators enable customers to translate needs into product specifications; typically via online configuration and visualization[25]
Citation: Towards Understanding Customer Co-creation Experience for Mass Customization. Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing, 2020. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-51828-8_19[25]

Configurable System: Participation Blueprint (PBP): framework/tool for configuring user participation in living labs; illustrated with a digital communication service co-designed with housing-complex residents[26]
Domain Context: Living labs / community innovation (case example in a housing complex; living labs applied across fields including healthcare and smart cities)[26]
Study Type: Literature review synthesizing living lab case studies to develop a framework for configuring participation[26]
Conceptual Framework: Participation Blueprint (PBP) framework with visual representations; identifies five categories and 11 elements for configuring participation in living labs[26]
Findings Implications: Identifies key elements to consider in configuring user participation[26]; PBP helps practitioners reflect on appropriateness and diversity of planned participation processes[26]
User Population: Local people (neighbourhood association members and residents) co-designing a digital communication service; generally living lab users as co-creative partners across stages[26]
Personalization Method: Configures “points of participation” by specifying elements in the PBP; includes selecting/combining participation formats such as online questionnaires and workshops[26]
Citation: Framework proposing the Participation Blueprint (PBP) for configuring participation in living labs (full bibliographic details not included in provided excerpts).[26]

Configurable System: Web-based house configurator: consolidated online configurator providing a customizable 3D house model; product and sales configurators are not coupled[27]
Domain Context: Engineer-to-order construction business providing customized house solutions[27]
Study Type: Design science research with case study method to analyze proposed methods[27]
Conceptual Framework: User-centered design framework for configuration systems; adapts Product Variant Master (PVM) model to represent knowledge from the user perspective; follows design thinking/double-diamond process[27]
Findings Implications: User involvement during development improves acceptance and use promotion of configurators[27]; reduced configuration and quote/BoM generation time (4h → 1h detailed; 30 min basic)[27]; mapping user features into the model supports monitoring/recording changes and describing different UIs via defaults and attribute characterization[27]
User Population: Configurator user is a technician; user expertise on house elements is medium to low[27]
Personalization Method: Knowledge-model attribute characterization (positive for user-input dependent vs negative for hidden/read-only attributes) and default values used to support different user interfaces and reduce variables/time[27]
Citation: Irene Campo Gay and Lars Hvam. Integrating User-Centered practices in Configuration Systems development: Framework and Conceptual Modelling. 2021.[27]

Configurable System: GUI for a housing co-design system enabling inhabitants to interact with a generative design backend; includes phase toolbar, 2D/3D main screen, and option library for customization[28]
Domain Context: Collective housing / housing cooperatives—digital tools for housing customization via co-design[28]
Study Type: Design research: defined, prototyped, and tested a GUI with experts, potential users, and architects[28]
Conceptual Framework: Framework on participation/co-design and use of digital technologies for housing customization[28]; follows user-centred design principles[28]; uses generative design system that produces viable solutions according to user preferences[28]
Findings Implications: Interface rated user-friendly/easy to use with high usability scores[28], including SUS total score 93.17[28]; tool shows potential to improve end-user participation in collective housing processes[28]
User Population: Potential users/inhabitants (30 participants; ages 25–45) and professionals/architects involved via interviews and evaluations[28]
Personalization Method: Generative design presents options for users to choose/customize based on preferences[28]; users drag predefined options from a library into the design[28]
Citation: Bridging the gap in customised housing design: Integrating a graphic user interface for user collaboration.[28]

Configurable System: Open value network (Sensorica) enabling online collaborative design of an open-source, modular solar PV characterisation apparatus with public documentation and GitHub-hosted code[29]
Domain Context: Other domain—open source scientific hardware / research instrumentation (photovoltaic characterisation apparatus)[29]
Study Type: Design research case study analyzing design and production of an open source scientific instrument within an open value network[29]
Conceptual Framework: Commons-based peer production and open value networks (OVN)[29]; participatory design infrastructuring concept (long-term, open-ended community processes)[29]
Findings Implications: Community participation and outreach were challenging (dropouts after ideation)[29]; accountability issues delayed delivery (anyone could stop participating)[29]; recommends clearer project objectives/expectations and governance mechanisms[29]
User Population: Diverse Sensorica members (design, communication, software, hardware) and makers/communities worldwide[29]
Personalization Method: Modular design supports repair/replacement/exchange/upgrade[29]; open documentation (documents, BOMs, process videos) and software code on GitHub enable remixing/local modification[29]
Citation: Democratising Design in Scientific Innovation: Application of an Open Value Network to Open Source Hardware Design.[29]
